strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem (memory-constrained deployment of GBDTs on microcontrollers) with a coherent combination of training-time regularizers and a specialized bit-wise memory layout with shared global threshold/leaf-value arrays.
The modified gain (Appendix A) is cleanly derived and integrates the feature/threshold penalties into the standard XGBoost/LightGBM boosting objective.

Extensive empirical study: three experiment types (baseline comparison, univariate and multivariate sensitivity analyses) across eight datasets, with 32k models per dataset in the grid search, and ablation-like isolation of the two penalties (reuse factor analysis is a nice touch).
Reported compression ratios of 4–16x at matched accuracy against LightGBM, quantized LightGBM, CEGB, and CCP baselines are meaningful, and the anonymous code repository supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the feature-cost regularizer is essentially an extension of CEGB (Peter et al., 2017), which the authors acknowledge; the threshold penalty and memory layout are useful but incremental engineering contributions rather than a fundamentally new technique.

No actual deployment or inference-time evaluation on microcontrollers despite the TinyML motivation; there are no latency, energy, or real-hardware measurements, and the memory accounting is analytical rather than measured on-device.

Missing comparisons against several directly relevant and recent baselines that the paper itself cites: post-training pruning/compression methods (Buschjäger & Morik 2023, Devos et al. 2025, Emine et al. 2025), Bonsai (Kumar et al., 2017), and compact multi-class boosting (Ponomareva et al., 2017). The empirical claim of superiority is only established against LightGBM variants, CEGB, and CCP.

Potential evaluation validity concern: models are selected as 'best-performing' from a massive grid search, and it is unclear whether this selection uses test-set performance; if so, the reported accuracies for ToaD (and baselines trained with the same grid) are optimistically biased. A single 80/20 split with no cross-validation or variance reporting compounds this.

High practical tuning burden: two extra hyperparameters (ι, ξ) require a large per-dataset, per-memory-limit grid search (32,076 models per dataset), which is a significant usability limitation for the intended practitioner audience and is not addressed with any heuristic or automatic selection procedure.

The 4–16x compression headline conflates two effects: part of the gain comes from the penalized training (which trades accuracy for size, standard in pruning) and part from the memory layout (which any trained model could use); a cleaner decomposition of where the savings come from would strengthen the claims.

Several presentation issues: Figure 3 is dense and hard to parse, the multiclass memory results are only partially explained, and writing errors (e.g., 'hyperparaneters', 'in constrast', duplicated sentence in Appendix D.1) suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: Addresses a practical and relevant problem: reducing the memory footprint of gradient-boosted tree ensembles for TinyML/IoT deployment on microcontrollers.

The technical contribution is concrete and well-specified: a modified gain function (Eq. 3, with derivations in Appendix A) that penalizes new features and thresholds during training, combined with a bit-wise, pointer-less memory layout using global feature/threshold/leaf-value lookup tables.

Extensive experimental protocol: large grid searches (~32,076 models per dataset), univariate and multivariate sensitivity analyses of the two penalty hyperparameters, and a useful 'reuse factor' metric to characterize threshold sharing.

Reasonable baseline comparison against LightGBM (float32 and FP16-quantized), CEGB, and cost-complexity pruning across eight public datasets, with reported 4–16x memory reductions at comparable accuracy.
Promises publicly available source code, including a 'forestsize' parameter for training under explicit memory budgets, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the approach is a fairly direct extension of Peter et al. (2017) (CEGB), adding a threshold penalty on top of the existing feature-cost idea, plus a bit-packing memory layout that is primarily engineering rather than a new scientific insight. No theoretical analysis of the trade-off or compression bounds is provided.

The central motivating claim (deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers) is never actually validated: there are no on-device experiments, no inference latency, energy, or RAM measurements on any microcontroller. All results are based on analytical memory accounting, and the paper itself concedes hardware deployment is future work.

Potential evaluation flaw: the 'best-performing model at each memory limit' is selected from the grid search, but it is unclear whether this selection is done on the test set. If so, the reported quality-memory frontiers for ToaD (and baselines) may be optimistically biased; the 80/20 single split with no cross-validation or variance reporting compounds this concern.

Missing comparison to recent, directly relevant compression baselines that the authors themselves cite (Devos et al., 2025; Emine et al., 2025; Buschjäger & Morik, 2023 as an actual method rather than only a memory-accounting convention), as well as stronger quantization approaches. The 128-bits-per-node baseline accounting is simplistic and may inflate the apparent compression advantage.

The gains conflate two effects (training regularization vs. encoding scheme). Although 'ToaD w/o Penalties' vs 'w/ Penalties' partially disentangles this, the baselines do not benefit from any bit-level packing, so the claimed 4–16x advantage over LightGBM largely reflects an unfair storage comparison rather than better learned models alone.
Only eight small-to-medium UCI-style datasets; no scale or diversity stress test, and practical questions (decode overhead of variable bit-width fields at inference, MCU code size) are unaddressed.

Presentation issues: typos and grammar errors ('hyperparaneters', 'In constrast', 'loop up'), a confusing Appendix B dataset description, and dense figures (e.g., Figures 6–7 and the appendix grids) that are hard to read at print resolution.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem (memory-constrained TinyML deployment of GBDTs) with a coherent end-to-end contribution: training-time regularizers that encourage reuse of features and thresholds, combined with a specialized bit-wise, pointer-less memory layout with global shared threshold/leaf-value arrays.

The derivation of the modified split gain (Appendix A) is clean and correctly integrates the new penalties into the standard XGBoost/LightGBM objective, building naturally on CEGB (Peter et al., 2017) with an additional, well-motivated threshold cost.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: a large hyperparameter grid (~32,076 models per dataset) across eight datasets spanning binary, multiclass, and regression tasks, plus dedicated univariate and multivariate sensitivity analyses of the two penalties, including an interpretable reuse-factor metric.

Results are convincing where they matter: in the 128 KB regime relevant to microcontrollers, baselines need 4–16x more memory to match ToaD's performance (e.g., covertype multiclass at 2 KB vs. 8–16 KB for quantized/float LightGBM), and the analysis usefully identifies Pareto-like trade-off points for penalty selection.

The framework is implemented on top of LightGBM (including a forest-size memory constraint parameter), and an anonymous repository with reproduction scripts is provided, supporting reproducibility. Limitations and LLM usage are disclosed transparently.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the feature-cost idea is a direct extension of cost-efficient gradient boosting (Peter et al., 2017), and pointer-less array-based tree encodings are standard engineering; the main novelty lies in the threshold penalty and the specific memory layout, which is more of a systems contribution than a methodological breakthrough.

A significant part of the compression appears to come from the memory layout alone (the 'ToaD w/o Penalties' baseline is competitive in Figure 4), which weakens the claim that the training regularizers are the key contribution and raises the question of whether the layout could simply be applied post-hoc to any trained LightGBM model.

Potential selection bias: the 'best-performing models' at each memory limit appear to be selected from grid-search results measured on the test set, which can inflate reported accuracy; there is no validation/test split for hyperparameter selection, no cross-validation (single 80/20 split), and no error bars or significance testing.

No actual deployment: despite the IoT/TinyML motivation, there are no measurements on real microcontrollers (RAM/flash usage, inference latency, energy consumption); all memory figures are analytical estimates based on bit-counting, so the central practical claim of autonomous on-device operation is not directly validated.

Baseline coverage is incomplete: recent competing post-training compression methods (Devos et al., 2025; Emine et al., 2025) are discussed in related work but not empirically compared; the memory accounting for baselines (128/64 bits per node) follows prior work but involves assumptions that may not favor the baselines.

Several claims are qualitative and rely on dense figures that are hard to read (Figures 4, 6, 7); a tabular summary of the headline compression ratios with confidence intervals would strengthen the evidence. Minor issues: typos ('hyperparaneters', 'In constrast'), and the Appendix D description contains duplicated sentences.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: memory-constrained deployment of GBDTs on microcontrollers is a practically relevant setting in TinyML.

The paper combines two complementary directions: training-time regularizers that encourage reuse of features and thresholds (extending CEGB-style cost penalties to threshold counts and encoding size), and a careful bit-level memory layout with global threshold/leaf arrays and pointer-less trees. The combination is coherent and the derivations (modified gain) are correct.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 8 datasets, multiple baselines (LightGBM float32/FP16/array-based, CEGB, CCP, plus RFs and pruned RFs in the appendix), 12 train-test splits, large grid searches (~32k models/dataset), plus univariate and multivariate sensitivity analyses and a reuse-factor metric.
Reported 4-16x compression at comparable accuracy is meaningful for the target domain, and ToaD beats array-based LightGBM, showing gains beyond mere pointer removal.

Honest reporting of limitations: prototype inference is 5-8x slower than LightGBM, multiclass uses one ensemble per class, and runtime experiments are presented as preliminary. Code and prototypes are released with versioned releases.
Good clarity overall; Figures 2-3 make the memory layout concrete.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: the core training-time idea is a direct extension of Peter et al. (2017) CEGB (feature-cost penalties), and threshold-sharing/bitlevel encodings exist in related work (QuickScorer variants, bit-level GBDT data structures). The main genuinely new elements are the threshold penalty and the specific global-array layout, which are more engineering than conceptual contributions.

Potential model-selection concern: for the headline comparison (Figure 4), the best-performing model at each memory limit is picked from the grid search. It is not fully clarified whether this selection uses validation or test performance; if the test set is used, the reported advantages may be inflated. This needs explicit clarification.

The memory accounting rules are defined by the authors (e.g., assuming complete trees, no leaf-class bits, node structure choices), which can favor ToaD over baselines; the fairness of the 128/64-bit-per-node accounting for competitors is debatable.

Datasets are small/mid-sized standard UCI benchmarks with modest feature counts (8-54); the claimed benefit of feature-index reuse may behave differently on high-dimensional or sparse data. No experiment with a 'real' IoT sensor dataset.

Hyperparameter guidance is largely empirical and dataset-dependent (two new hyperparameters must be tuned via grid search), which reduces practical ease-of-use; the authors themselves state there is no globally optimal setting.
Only preliminary microcontroller deployment results in the appendix; the claim that latency/energy impact is negligible is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Some presentation issues: inconsistencies in notation across Section 3.1 and Appendix A, figure 6/7 descriptions dense, and the 'reuse of leaf values' mechanism is discussed but not effectively regularized (acknowledged in conclusion).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (memory-constrained deployment of GBDTs on microcontrollers) and the proposed solution is technically plausible and well-motivated.

Extensive experimental protocol: 8 datasets, 12 random splits, a very large hyperparameter grid (~32k models per dataset), plus univariate and multivariate sensitivity analyses of the two penalty parameters, including a novel reuse-factor metric.

Comparison against several baselines (LightGBM in standard, FP16, and array-based variants, CCP pruning, CEGB, and RF baselines in the appendix), and the array-based LightGBM control helps isolate the benefit of the encoding beyond a pointer-less layout.
Good reproducibility: code built on LightGBM, documented seeds, datasets, a release version, and prototype microcontroller deployments.
The sensitivity analyses provide useful practical guidance (e.g., ReF peaks, penalty ranges) beyond a single headline result.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core training modification is a direct extension of CEGB (Peter et al., 2017): the modified gain in Eq. (3)/(7)-(8) is exactly CEGB's cost-augmented gain with thresholds added as a second cost term, and the derivation (Appendix A) is straightforward. The remaining contribution is a bit-level memory layout (pointer-less arrays, shared threshold/leaf tables, per-feature bit widths), which is largely engineering and closely related to prior bit-level structures (QuickScorer variants, Devos et al., Koschel et al.), so the conceptual advance over existing work is modest.

Missing comparisons with state-of-the-art compression methods. The paper cites strong recent baselines (Buschjäger & Morik 2023, Devos et al. 2025, Emine et al. 2025, Liu & Mazumder 2023 / ForestPrune) but does not compare against any of them, only against plain LightGBM, CCP, and CEGB. The 4–16x claim is therefore only established against relatively weak baselines.

Potential selection bias in the headline comparison: the best ToaD model at each memory limit is picked from a 32,076-model grid search, while baselines are trained with a much smaller hyperparameter set. Even with a validation split, this asymmetric search budget makes the quality-vs-memory curves difficult to interpret fairly, and the practical cost of finding good penalty settings (acknowledged in Section 4.4 as dataset-dependent) is underplayed.

Compression accounting questions: leaf values are stored at fixed 32-bit precision, which typically dominates GBDT memory; the paper does not analyze how much of the gain comes from the penalties vs. the layout vs. avoiding float32 in thresholds, and no leaf-value quantization baseline is considered. The metadata overhead of the Feature & Threshold Map is also not quantified.

Deployment evidence is thin: microcontroller experiments (Appendix E.1) show a 5–8x inference slowdown, and claims about negligible latency/energy impact are asserted rather than measured; multiclass handling (one ensemble per class) is unoptimized and explicitly left to future work.

Presentation issues: several typos ('leafs', 'constrast', 'hyperparamter', 'values seem'), Figure 3 is cluttered and hard to follow, and the abstract's 'same performance with 4–16x compression' claim is stronger than what the regression results (where competitors catch up at larger memory budgets) support.

strengths: Clear and relevant problem: memory-footprint reduction of GBDTs for TinyML/IoT deployment is a practically significant task, and the paper is well-motivated with concrete hardware constraints (e.g., 32 KB RAM microcontrollers).

The proposed approach is coherent and technically sound: feature/threshold reuse penalties are cleanly integrated into the gain computation (with derivation in Appendix A), and the bit-wise memory layout with global threshold/leaf-value arrays and pointer-less trees is well described and illustrated (Figures 2-3).

Extensive and convincing evaluation: a large grid search (32,076 models per dataset) across eight datasets, comparison to multiple reasonable baselines (LightGBM float32/FP16/array-based, CEGB, CCP, and RFs in the appendix), univariate and multivariate sensitivity analyses of both penalties, and a reuse-factor metric that helps interpret the mechanism.

Empirically strong results: consistent 4-16x compression at matched performance, with a concrete example (Covertype multiclass: 69% accuracy at 2 KB vs. 8 KB for quantized LightGBM), and results across binary, multiclass, and regression tasks.

Good reproducibility: implementation on top of LightGBM, code and experiment scripts released, seeds and dataset references documented, plus prototype deployment on two microcontrollers with measured runtimes (Table 2) providing honest reporting of the 5-8x inference slowdown.
Honest scoping: the paper clearly states that memory, not latency/energy, is the target bottleneck, and discusses limitations and future work.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea directly extends CEGB (Peter et al., 2017) by adding feature-encoding-cost and threshold penalties, and pointer-less/array-based tree storage, shared threshold tables, and quantization are largely standard engineering techniques. The contribution is more a well-executed combination than a fundamentally new method.

Stronger or more recent post-training compression baselines (e.g., Devos et al., 2025; Emine et al., 2025; Buschjäger & Morik, 2023; Liu & Mazumder, 2023) are cited and discussed but not empirically compared, which weakens the claim that the training-time approach is preferable to state-of-the-art pruning/compression.

Potential selection bias in the headline comparison: the 'best model' at each memory limit is picked from the grid search, and it is not entirely clear this selection uses only validation data; if test performance informed model selection, reported gains could be inflated (applied uniformly to baselines, but the concern remains for the magnitude of the compression ratios).

Two additional hyperparameters (ι, ξ) must be tuned per dataset/memory budget; the paper acknowledges there is no globally optimal setting and provides only heuristic guidance (penalties ≥ 1, ≥ 32 for larger datasets), which increases practical deployment burden.
Multiclass classification uses one ensemble per class, which multiplies memory; the paper notes ToaD is not yet optimized for multiclass, yet multiclass results are among the headline claims.

Inference latency is 5-8x slower than LightGBM on microcontrollers (Appendix E.1); the argument that latency is negligible in real deployments is plausible but only preliminary, and the runtime study is small (one dataset, one model, random inputs).
Scope of datasets is modest (eight UCI-style tabular sets, largest ~580k instances); generalization to very high-dimensional or streaming settings is untested.
